CausalChain: Tumor stress (hypoxia/oxidative stress) -> Upregulation of specific tRF biogenesis -> Selective binding with RNA-binding proteins for exosomal sorting -> Stress-induced exosomal surface modifications -> Selective exosome uptake by macrophages -> Intracellular binding of tRFs to RNA-binding proteins -> Altered mRNA stability/translation and gene expression in macrophages -> M2-like (immunosuppressive) polarization -> Enhanced tumor progression and metastasis
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that under tumor stress conditions, cancer cells generate a unique suite of tRFs that are selectively sorted into exosomes through interactions with specific RNA-binding proteins. These interactions not only determine the RNA cargo but also induce post-translational modifications on exosomal surfaces that promote their selective uptake by tumor-associated macrophages. Once internalized, the tRFs engage with intracellular RNA-binding proteins, altering mRNA stability and translation, which reprograms macrophages into an immunosuppressive, M2-like state that drives tumor progression and metastasis. This hypothesis will be tested using integrated advanced techniques including high-resolution exosome proteomics, RNA interactome methods, single-cell transcriptomics, CRISPR-Cas9 functional screens, and live imaging modalities to capture the dynamics of tRF-mediated signaling in the tumor microenvironment.
Abstract: Our refined hypothesis proposes that under tumor stress conditions, such as hypoxia and oxidative stress, cancer cells not only upregulate the production of a distinct subset of tRNA-derived fragments (tRFs) but also facilitate their selective packaging into exosomes via sophisticated, RNA-binding protein (RBP)-mediated sorting mechanisms. These exosomes acquire unique surface markers—through stress-induced post-translational modifications—that target them for preferential uptake by tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs). Once internalized, the tRFs interact with specific intracellular RBPs, modulating the stability and translation of key mRNAs and thereby reprogramming macrophages into an immunosuppressive, M2-like phenotype that supports tumor progression and metastasis. Leveraging cutting-edge methodologies such as high-resolution exosome proteomics, RNA interactome capture, single-cell transcriptomics, CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screens, and advanced in vivo imaging, each step of this cascade can be quantitatively and temporally dissected, paving the way for novel therapeutic interventions in cancer immunomodulation.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis focused on the generation and exosomal transfer of tRFs from cancer cells to reprogram TAMs. In our revised version, we have enhanced mechanistic clarity by: (1) explicitly incorporating the role of stress-induced post-translational modifications in creating exosome surface markers that facilitate selective macrophage uptake; (2) detailing the interaction of tRFs with intracellular RBPs to alter mRNA stability and translation, thereby offering more precise insights into the mechanism of macrophage reprogramming; (3) emphasizing the use of contemporary technologies (exosome proteomics, RNA interactome capture, CRISPR-Cas9 screens, and advanced imaging) that allow for quantitative and temporal dissection of each causal step. This refined causal chain explicitly reflects each step of the original reasoning while addressing key gaps and enhancing both innovation and experimental feasibility.
